summary: 88 new person entries chosen to rebalance a timeline that was three-quarters men (user decision 2026-11-01: the thesis-count bar was dropped for women and non-binary scholars; target about 40%), with 927 relationships, 239 roster rows and 968 sources. Researched by Sol 6.1 (Codex) and Claude researchers; every relationship was checked against its cited passage by independent Claude verification agents; Fable 5.1, GPT and Gemini reviewed the full candidate and their findings were applied. Also: typo, Indigenous-framing and date fixes to existing entries and edges, and six older edges re-pointed to the new person entries they described.
authorization: User, 2026-11-01: "I think we drop the bar for women or nonbinary scholars to help push towards 40%"; approved the candidate list, review by Fable, Gemini and GPT, "we should do all the easy clear fixes"; 2026-11-02: "you can push to the live site". Research, verification and review records stay in the research folder.
rationale: The timeline drew its person entries mainly by dissertation-citation counts, which left it 75% men and structurally under-ranked the founders of women's and gender history. This revision adds women historians and theorists with verified relationships in both directions, so they sit inside the network rather than at its edge.

edge_1804.relationship: As Hannah Tandy documents from Woodward’s 1938 letter, Black Reconstruction supplied an acknowledged scholarly debt.

edge_1886.relationship: As Buckner reconstructs the 1997 argument, Owram calls for studying how regional and local identities interact within a shared national experience while rejecting a return to a patriotic elite’s master narrative.

edge_1970.relationship: Wood objects that Turner’s 1895 account of American origins leaves Indigenous people outside its historical explanation.

edge_2275.relationship: Winter challenges Ferguson’s confident counterfactual account of British nonintervention in 1914 as exceeding the available evidence.

edge_2357.relationship: Questions the internalist/externalist division associated with Kuhn’s 1968 history-of-science essay, treating the boundary itself as a historical problem.

edge_2527.relationship: Foner credits Thompson’s social history with helping him integrate ideas and social conflict, and uses The Making of the English Working Class to link class formation with political exclusion and the struggle for the vote.

edge_2530.relationship: Foner criticizes the exaggerated elitism and distrust of mass politics in Hofstadter’s accounts of Populism and reform, while crediting their analytical innovations and distinguishing his critical consensus history from celebratory versions.

edge_2531.relationship: Foner questions whether White’s Greater Reconstruction framework homogenizes federal action in the South and West, and argues that its emphasis on defeat and violence gives too little attention to Black political leaders.

edge_2536.relationship: Furet disputes Marx’s account of the Terror as a plebeian way of completing the bourgeois revolution, arguing that its essential transformation was already achieved in 1789–1791.

edge_901.relationship: Ecological change as a two-way relation of people and nature, traced through property, markets and ideas of nature (1983–1995); and the field's institutions: ASEH president 1989–93, editor of the Weyerhaeuser Environmental Books 1994–2014 ('acquiring, editing, and writing forewords for all titles'), and, as AHA president (2012; presidential address January 2013), 'the first self-described environmental historian ever to serve as president of the AHA'
